utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, to you Mr. Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. For the record, all the accused are here. Presentation is exactly as it was yesterday. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We just wants to thank the court for its indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. On our part we want to make sure that your client is feeling fit to continue attending the sitting at any time, so we are informing him that if at any time he needs a break or he needs to leave the courtroom or there's anything wrong, he will just need to draw our attention and we will attend to his needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I know he is aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nikolic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic will be proceeding with his cross-examination and then we'll start with that of the Beara Defence team. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before I start my cross-examination I'd like to indicate two translation errors in my questions yesterday. The first one is on the page 33003, line 11. It's the word "events." I used at this point in time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, do you have the page number of the day instead of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you start from page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From page 1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My LiveNote hasn't been updated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah. It is 33, page 33 line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The word -- B/C/S word "odluke," as decisions, was translated as "events" and it was quoted from statement, the written statement of the witness. And in the other -- my other question was on the page 56, line 1, or the page 025 of updated transcript. Line 22 and 23. Just a moment. It is after the word "to secure," I used the B/C/S word "zive ljude." It was live people. Free people. But it was translated as "area," as "the area."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in your mind there is no problem with Mr. Nikolic having misunderstood your questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, we can now proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We left off yesterday on the issue of the relocation of graves that you talked about. You named the units or part of the units that were involved in the carrying out of this task, and generally speaking who participated in that operation when you were being questioned by the OTP. Among other things, you mentioned the engineering unit of the Drina Corps as one of the participants. My question is, do you know whether the engineering corps from your brigade took part in that as well.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just for your information the Bratunac Brigade didn't have any engineering corps of that type necessary for any sort of excavation works relating to the relocation of graves. There was a young lieutenant or second lieutenant in the engineering part but nothing more than that, and, of course, I'm sorry, I would like to add this, there was also a group of engineering troops who were in charge of planting mines or demining and opening passages and things like that. There was nothing else other than that in the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that fuel had been provided by the corps and that your duty was to keep records of the consumption of the fuel. That's what you said the day before yesterday in the examination-in-chief. Now, concerning this, I'd like to ask you the following, because there is something a little bit unclear to me and if you can help me with that. What was the reason for the Drina Corps command to issue fuel to the Bratunac Brigade so that the Bratunac Brigade would then pass it on to the engineering corps of the Drina Corps? Can you offer any explanation of the reasons why didn't they do it directly? Why didn't they give it directly to the engineers battalion and appoint one of their people to keep track?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Apparently you have oversimplified this issue. Within the framework of the operation, not only the machines from the engineering battalion, from Konjevic Polje was engaged, and which was part of the Drina Corps establishment, many machines were engaged in this operation. If you are interested, I can name you all the organisations that supplied machines engaged in these works. There is nothing unusual or illogical in the fact that among all these machines there was an excavator. I don't know what type of the machine it was, and that it spent a certain period of time carrying out works assigned to the Bratunac Brigade. Like everybody else who took part in this operation, took fuel from the gas station or the petrol station where it was stored. So I don't see anything unusual for a machine from an engineering unit that belongs to the Drina Corps tanked their machines at the same point as everybody else who took part in this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you didn't understand my question fully. The essence of my question was why do you think it was you who were appointed to keep track of the consumption of the fuel issued among other units to the 5th Battalion of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yeah, I can explain it to you. There is no separation of fuel for the engineering unit of the corps. The issue is about two lots of fuel that we received. The first one was 5 tonnes, the next one was 3 tonnes. It was supplied to the Bratunac Brigade for the execution of this particular task. There were no separate tasks involved. This was a one operation, a single operation, in which machines mainly provided by work organisations from the municipalities of Bratunac and Srebrenica who had these machines available. The only machine engaged in these works for a certain period of time was an excavator driven by a man whose name I don't know, but his nickname was Caruga. He was a professional driver living in Milici. He was in this unit at the time and he drove this machine and he came to fill his tank. As for monitoring the use of the fuel, that was how it was. There was a terrible shortage of fuel at the time, and why this decision was made to have the security organ monitor the consumption of fuel and then after the completion of the operation to hand over reports with all the records of the use of fuel. All these logs contain the number of the machine, the dates, the quantities of the fuel issued and the signature of the authorised person. All these logs relating to the issue and consumption of fuel after the operation was finished, I handed over to the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, you have given us a good explanation, a detailed explanation. [In English] Translation, I -- oh, sorry. Yeah, okay. It's correct. [Interpretation] In this operation which was called "asnacija," did Miroslav Deronjic have any role in it, and if he did, what was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can tell you in general terms what kind of role the political structures from Bratunac played, and he was part of that structure. I don't know in which way, but they too were involved in all of this from the very outset. Those were Miroslav Deronjic as the president of the SDS, and the then, I think, still an envoy of the president relating to civilian affairs in Srebrenica. Then Srbislav Davidovic, the chairman of the executive council was also activity involved. The president of the municipality assembly of Bratunac, Mr. Ljubisa Simic, and chief of the public security station in Bratunac, Mr. Miodrag Josipovic. In addition to these people from the political structure, also included was the entire economy or, rather, the companies that had construction machinery available.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm for the moment interested only in the role of Mr. Deronjic. Can you tell me more precisely during this operation, did you ever seek any assistance from him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I asked him to get in touch with representatives of the political authorities because that simply wasn't my duty. Of course, I could have done that, but I couldn't influence them and make them talk and become involved in try to engage the companies in Bratunac. I wasn't able to achieve that and that's why I talked to Mr. Deronjic. Naturally I did that on the authorisation of my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts with him regarding the engagement of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read out to you a portion of the statement given here by a protected witness on the 19th of November, 2007, and this witness number 170. And that's on page 17857, lines 17 to 21. "[In English] The witness said that in September or October 1995, Deronjic informed the witness that the workers were needed and that they should report to Momir Nikolic at the Bratunac Brigade command around 9.00 p.m. or 10.00 p.m. The witness accompanied the man and turned them over to Momir Nikolic in front of the brigade command."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure but judging from the manner in which this is written, and I know that it happened yesterday as well, so I want to bring it to my learned friend's attention, it could be that he is reading a summary, in which case I don't think that's the proper practice. I think the substance, whatever it actually is, should be put to the witness, not a summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was quoted from the transcript, and it might be a summary but it was admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can safely go ahead. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it's not evidence. We may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me next whether this accurately reflects the events that the witness referred to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You read out a small portion of text to me and you are asking me whether it reflects the totality of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you to do.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Then please be more precise in what it is that you are asking from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is whether you recall the event referred to by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what witness you are talking about. If I knew his identity, I could give you more precise statement about it. In any case, I do not dispute that at the beginning of the operation, which was termed "asnacija" in my brigade, people were coming in and reporting to me. I participated in the operation. I was a witness to it, and I do not deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that it was sent to you by Mr. -- that they were sent to you by Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, he could have. I cannot exclude the possibility that he was involved, but there was no possibility for me to know that Deronjic was sending them over. I don't think it was the case, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The day before yesterday you spoke about sniping, the sniping of civilians, as you said, in Srebrenica. On such occasions, were people who were in Srebrenica itself targeted, or were those people in the proximity of the separation line?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is an unclear question. I have to be more precise in my answer. The sniping beginning with the establishment or the enclave until the fall of the town, people were being targeted by snipers. Those people who were in front of the lines of the Bratunac Brigade as well as the Skelani Battalion and the Milici Brigade. People were targeted who were immediately in front of the lines occupied by members of the Bratunac Brigade. This is what I can talk about. As for the sniping in Srebrenica itself, that was not possible because there were no technical means to conduct any sniping campaigns in the town of Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said in front of the lines of the Bratunac and other brigades of the VRS. Were there any Muslim lines or the lines of the army of B&H there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So when you say that there was sniping from the frontlines of the VRS units including the Bratunac Brigade, does that mean that there were targeting the lines of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe a distinction needs to be made to make things clear. I'm not talking about exchanges of fire which happened daily. That was not an issue. I am talking about the sniping of civilians in the enclave because of which I frequently had to discuss this with members of DutchBat as well as with military monitors because they came with first and last names of those who were unarmed and were killed just in front of, say, the 2nd Infantry Battalion. Such cases happened in the other battalions as well, such as the 3rd. The same applies the other way around, meaning to say that from the demilitarised zone, members of the 28th Division round the clock were conducting sniping activity. They would approach the lines of the Serb forces killing the soldiers there as well as the civilians who happened to be in the proximity of the lines because they had property there. This was a daily problem for me as the liaison officer. I was supposed to explain what it was that was being targeted from the frontlines endangering the demilitarised zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As for the locations of sniping, where the two lines were between the separated armies of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the VRS, who were these civilians that would be in this area in the no-man's land or just immediately behind the lines of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were targeted? In other words, my question is, did the DutchBat members that you spoke to explain to you who those civilians were and what they were doing between the lines or immediately behind the lines of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina since one would expect fire to be opened?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think you understand or are grasping the concept fully, that there is a frontline and there's nobody around it. Those were inhabited areas. Let's take the example of Budak village. All of the local residents lived there, the lines, the trenches in the area of Budak were in the village itself or in its outskirts, and people had their property, their land which they worked, because they were living there. There was no strict division between the line where the soldiers were of the Muslim army and the soldiers of the VRS with an area which would be empty, void of any living being. People lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your conversations with the members of DutchBat, did they ever tell that you a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was targeted by snipers?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They were targeted, both members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and ... But let me tell you this, they never complained of people who were targeted because they carried arms. If they themselves came across such people who sported arms, they would disarm them. They knew there were armed people. They even had problems in certain areas. For example, in the area of Suceska they had grave problems with the formation of Zulfo Tursunovic. He was a commander there and commanded a unit which they never managed to disarm. This is no secret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, to interrupt you Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Nikolic, as for the sniping the Muslim civilians by the VRS, it's not clear to me how you became aware of it. Did you mean that you became aware of it due to the complaint by the DutchBat as well as the monitors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among other sources, it was thanks to them as well. But to be completely clear in all companies and all units I had my people. In each battalion I had an assistant, or rather the commander had his assistant for security and intelligence, and that person would inform me of such incidents. Therefore, I had that source, the people who were working along my professional line, then the battalion commanders reported to the brigade commander on any breaches of cease-fire. And the third source were members of the DutchBat and the international observers who were there, and they followed up on any incident that had to deal with sniping. Therefore, I had full information about cease-fire violations and the sniping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what I'm interested in is whether you heard from your subordinate or the fellow VRS officer or soldier that they purposefully targeted the civilians? Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right. Civilians were being targeted intentionally. You're right. I spoke to soldiers numerous times. I even talked to the brigade commander and he took full note of it. He even suggested that certain soldiers be brought into custody and proceedings initiated because they were sniping civilians, because those were not military targets. They were not armed soldiers, but people working the land, ploughing, fixing the roofs of their houses, and they became sniping targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether you could name those such sources who gave such information to you? If necessary, we can hear that in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What are you exactly asking me to tell you? Which names?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Those who told you that the VRS soldiers intentionally targeted Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you. One of the people I spoke with who was in charge of this area where there was sniping was Zoran Jovanovic, assistant commander for intelligence and security in the 2nd Infantry Battalion, and for awhile he was also battalion commander deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the interruption, but there's an important transcript error that I've been advised of. The witness apparently did not say that it was commander Blagojevic who had suggested that some of these people be brought into custody but rather it was Momir Nikolic himself who made that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've heard -- Mr. Nikolic, you've heard what Mr. Gosnell has just stated, and I see you nodding. Are you in agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I suggested to Commander Blagojevic, my brigade commander, to have those who conducted sniping and of whom we know -- we knew by their name to initiate disciplinary proceedings, and for them to be detained. That is what I suggested to Commander Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to follow-up concerning what you just said about Zoran Jovanovic. Did you receive information from him that he had ordered something to that effect, something like that to be done, or was it merely a piece of information he learned from someone else and conveyed it to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me that he had ordered it. Zoran Jovanovic for one thing would never order such a thing. I was just told that it was done without his approval. It was the behaviour of soldiers who were very difficult to control along the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke with the members of DutchBat since we've heard here that certain sabotage groups would leave the enclave and go through the lines of the VRS in order to sabotage military targets, but also to attack the civilian population in the nearby villages. Did you know of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was taking place on a large scale and each time I protested without reserve. I even suggested in the most problematic regions that DutchBat move their check-points, change the way they operated. I kept bugging at them non-stop to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The people carrying out such sabotage operations, were they usually in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot answer that, whether they were in civilian clothes. I didn't see them as they were doing that, therefore I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As an intelligence officer, did you receive information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If you are asking me whether I know what sort of clothes they wore, then I can tell you that they wore all sorts of clothes. They had civilian clothes, mixed civilian and military items, different types of uniform. I did, of course, have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that in discussions with members of DutchBat you received information that members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were also being targeted and that they did not protest that, it was my impression that they basically kept record of those who were members of the army and those who were not, otherwise how would they know who was and -- or who was not a civilian. Was that your impression as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think that is a plausible explanation in general terms. The fact that they knew there were armed people around, that is something that they were aware of as well. As for their assessments, well, as a person who worked on that, I provided my assessments. I don't know to what degree they were accurate, but as for their assessments, that I don't know. They were covering an area and they had a team of five intelligence people working on that, and you should put this question to them. I cannot tell you anything precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that they were aware of the existence of armed people. Were they aware of the existence of the organised defence by units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina which used to change the name, first it was called the 8th Operations Group, then it was named the 28th Division, so and within this division --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You are again asking me a hypothetical question. If you are asking me if they knew about these things, I don't know. If you are asking me what I think and if you rephrase your question, then I can give you an answer. Sorry, the state of mind of members of the DutchBat, that's something I cannot tell you anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever draw their attention at your meetings to your knowledge about the existence in Srebrenica of the 28th Division of an army? It's not just a group of armed people, armed people can be found in any situate town.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did and that was one of my tasks and duties. If I hadn't known that, then I shouldn't have been in that position and in that post. And I did draw their attention that according to the reports that I have and estimates that I have, that there were armed units. And then my duty was to report to my Superior Command, and then I received feedback instructions what to request from UNPROFOR and this is what I did. Of course, I didn't have an opportunity to make decisions myself about what to do, but whatever was asked of me from the superior command, I conveyed to UNPROFOR without fail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they ever tell you that there was no armed formation there, that there were only armed individuals? That there was no 28th Division or 8th Operations Group, brigades, commanders?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, in my conversations with members of the DutchBat and military observers, I never went into such discussions and debates and analyses. At the level at which I was, the crucial thing for me was that there were armed men ahead of us, that they were leaving the area of the enclave, that they were endangering the safety of the areas where they were moving, that they were coming close to the lines with sniper rifles and killing people. And I think that in one period 58 murders were committed from the enclave. And this is what I presented to the Dutch Battalion and international observers, and on that basis I asked things to be resolved and asked them to prevent any such exits from the enclave. About the existence of the 28th Division and the transformation of the 8th Operation Group into the 28th Division was my assessment on which I worked very extensively, and I adapted and adjusted my assessment based on each single piece of new information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us first correct one error in the transcript. You said that 58 murders were committed from the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Within one period when I kept a record, probably. I am not talking about the whole period when the enclave was declared until the fall of Srebrenica. For one period I kept track, and with this information and these figures I intervened with the Dutch battalion because I had arguments to show them that there was no peace in the enclave and that the Muslim forces had not been completely disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In order for us to be more precise, the victims of these 58 murders were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. And most of them were people killed on the lines. That is to say, members of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify one more issue. You said that your assessment about the existence of the 28th Division and the 8th Operations Group were -- can we say that this were the information shared with the VRS or was this your personal assessment?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course these are not my personal assessments. I did that for the purpose of the VRS, and I forwarded my findings to the command in charge, that is the Drina Corps command. Any new information that I gathered, I did that for the purposes of the military, not for my personal purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, let us conclude this topic, does that mean that the VRS knew about the existence of the 28th Division inside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am sure that that was identical to all other assessments in the VRS as a total.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement of facts, you spoke, among other things, about the killing of six Muslims on the 13th of July, 1995. You said that this was done by a military policeman by the name of Mile Petrovic, and that he even told you personally that that was his revenge for his brother or whoever, this is probably irrelevant at the moment. Do you still claim that this is how it happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I claim that what I said during my testimony and in my statement is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You had an opportunity to hear Mile Petrovic's testimony which took place during the deliberation on your sentence, and you heard him refute that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that he did not tell the truth then when he testified here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted) with regard to this incident they confirmed in principle. Of course, not in the same language and the same phrasing but the essence is totally identical except the fact that he did the killing. Now, I can tell you that there is not a single man, once you accuse him of murder that he would confess and say, yes, I did it. They did confirm everything and I'm convinced that the Trial Chamber believe that this incident did happen. And I still maintain that it happened in the way how I described it and that it had to do with the killing of these six men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that same occasion, actually in the same paragraph, you say that on the same day, that is the 13th of July, at around noon, you brought Resid Sinanovic to the Bratunac Brigade and that you handed him over it to Zlatko Celanovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what -- how did you explain to Celanovic while you were handing over Sinanovic precisely to him of all people?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please start his answer from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hold it, Mr. Nikolic. One moment, we've got problems with interpretation. Could I kindly ask you to start your answer fresh, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me clarify the whole situation surrounding Sinanovic. We had information and reports that Mr. Sinanovic was among those who had committed war crimes. When I arrived in Konjevic Polje, members of the civilian police who were manning the check-point in Konjevic Polje told me that Resid Sinanovic was in the area. After the time I spent in Konjevic Polje, I took Resid Sinanovic and drove him to the military police in Bratunac. I handed him over to Zlatan Celanovic, and as for Zlatan Celanovic, I mentioned that in my testimony before, was a lawyer, who worked in the Bratunac Brigade on the issues related to filing reports, gathering evidence about crimes, and was involved to a great extent in the questioning of all those who surrendered themselves or defectors who were taken prisoner from Srebrenica. Therefore, Zlatan Celanovic was an authorised person pursuant to the brigade commanders decision to conduct investigation, gather evidence, do the checks, and file criminal reports. Therefore, it was absolutely logical to me to hand this man over to him and to the military police who was of course supposed later on to apply the legal procedure. And let me just tell you one more thing. Everything that happened later on and for the sake of truth, Mr. Resid Sinanovic was not killed in Bratunac, he was not maltreated, he was allowed to receive visits by his friends from Bratunac, and after that, as far as I know, Zlatan Celanovic transferred him personally together with other prisoners to the Vuk Karadzic elementary school and he ended up in Zvornik. My lawyers investigated this whole case, and all the documents indicate that Resid Sinanovic was transferred to Zvornik where he got wounded, then he swam across the Drina and found himself in the hospital in Banja Koviljaca. We handed over all these documents to the OTP, Mr. McCloskey, and his team. So Mr. Sinanovic ended up as a patient in a hospital in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We had an opportunity to hear Mr. Celanovic as well, so I'm not going to ask you any more questions about this. Let's move on. You said that both Mirko Jankovic and Mile Petrovic had confirmed what you said; however, in the statement of be facts, among other things, it is written about Mirko Jankovic that while coming back with the APC on the 30th of July, he brought with him an amount of German marks and he explained that he had received that from the police by the road. Do you know that he also denied this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yeah, he can deny whatever he wants, I'm telling you what I saw with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pay a little bit more attention, because this guy was a protected witness and we are effecting a redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it's my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, you also mentioned the killing in Kravica or that the killings in Kravica were committed by Milovan Martic and Nikola Popovic among others. Are you aware that there was no proceedings instituted against Nikola Popovic and that Milovan Martic was acquitted?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My only task was to investigate whether any members of the Bratunac Brigade took part or were present during the commission of these killings. And I testified in the Martic case. I know that he was acquitted. And as for the fact that no indictment was issued against this other man, I really don't know. It was not up to me to decide. But I did mention these individuals who were on the spot when the murder took place, when the murders took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 11, you described a convoy of buses and trucks with prisoners moving from Bratunac to Zvornik, and you said that it was 1 and a half kilometres long convoy. Can you tell me how do you know that? How do you know how long the convoy was?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because I saw it, I saw this convoy moving on that day. Actually, it was formed in Bratunac and it was on the way to Zvornik. And on the road where the convoy was formed is the area from which I hail and I know it very well, but that would be my rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that you spoke with Mr. Mirko Jankovic on that same day. Did he tell you that he was only in one school in Zvornik when he escorted this convoy? Do you know, did he go to only one school as he said or did he go to more than one schools?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think I said that I received information from Mirko Jankovic pertaining to Pilica to leaving a police patrol behind, and Mirko Jankovic told me that he reached Zvornik and after escorting them, he just turned his APC and went back. Believe me, I never inquired anything further about that. I never asked him to tell me specifically what he saw or anything of that sort. Yes, we did discuss but without any detail and any specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put to you one portion of your interview given to the OTP, and it relates to your duties concerning prisoners. It's contained in your interview mentioned yesterday, pages 38 and 39, among other things, and I'm going to quote what you said: "I said that my task was to designate locations for gathering and detaining and securing prisoners." What I'm interested in at the moment is, what was the basis of the task given to you, or is what I have read correct and accurate? Do you remember saying this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do. As far as I am capable, I really do my best to give you answer to every question, so I worked at the staff for a period of time, I have certain education, as you know. I took part in exercises during peacetime. Well, it only shows that -- I should have learned what the task of an intelligence security service should be in wartime. I never acted, nor do I want to act now, as if I had never been in war, as if I hadn't ever known what my tasks or duties were, but equally, the tasks of an intelligence and security organ is what you described and I'm fully aware of what it should be doing in wartime. And these things are defined by an order or decision issued by a commander. However, whether it is -- if it is produced in a written form or not, I know what my duty is. And each organ is obliged to comply with duties that are stipulated by their post per establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned an order by the commander and we'll get to that, but do you recall any regulation that would oblige you to do what you have just discussed, i.e., to have any sort of authority over prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it is regulated by the rules of service of the security organ. I had an opportunity to go through the rules of service and I have not come across that, that's why I'm asking you. If you want me to answer this, I would have to refer to the rules and I believe I'd be able to locate that in the regulations. In any case, I won't argue because I don't have it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we perhaps find it in the rules of service of intelligence organs to have contact with prisoners, gather data, maybe if you are confusing the two documents?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am not going to assert what I'm not certain of. I think that prisoners are mentioned in both sets of rules, the rules of service of security organs, and the rules from 1978 concerning intelligence. If I had both, I'd be able to answer precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers must observe a pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zivanovic, Mr. Nikolic, please you are creating problems for the interpreters, if you could kindly observe a short pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, is it the time for break or we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The break will be at 10 minutes to 11.00. 10 minutes to 11.00. And I think your time is practically up. I think you better check, I'm going to check. Concentrate on important questions, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. All these questions are very important for our case, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will show you an order you had seen before. It is the order for active combat, P107. It is the very order that has to do the with operation in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go to page 5. Item 10. Sorry, I think it's the next page. No, no, it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the second paragraph which says, Security organs of the military police will designate the areas for prisoners of war and collection of war booty. It's one or two paragraphs that we are quite familiar with because we went through them on a number of occasions. Do you recall this? Do you recall these two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Before that I wanted to say that I had not seen this order before the operation. I saw it for the first time when I received it with the other documents received from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go to 1D382.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is the same order basically, save for a few things that were put in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go to the same page, I think it was page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the same order, the same text, it's just that the two paragraphs are crossed out, and in the upper part of the page on top, there is an annotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the entire top of the B/C/S shown. It says "Area of assembly of POWs," and "The area of Pribicevac," and on the very top it says "And war booty." Could we also have the right-hand side of the document shown, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The area of Pribicevac or is the area of Pribicevac. Do you know how it came about that these interventions were introduced?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I see this document with these handwritten notes for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We had occasion to hear Mr. Trisic who appeared as witness, I believe you know him, he testified on the 20th of October, 2008 at pages 27059, line 18, to page 27109, line 7. So as not to have to go through the whole testimony, I just wanted to share this with you, he stated that the changes on this document were made by you, the handwritten notes. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It should be up to you to conclude whether I as an officer of the Light Infantry Brigade, and I believe this was an order from the Drina Corps command, whether I would be in a position to change the contents of an order signed by the corps commander, General Zivanovic, if it was signed by him. We should go to the end of the order to see that. Do you really think that I was such a force, such an authority there to be able to change that? I'm telling you that I have no idea what this is about. First of all, I was never involved in this and it is difficult for me to even comprehend that type of statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you claim that you did not cross the paragraphs out and that you did not make the handwritten annotations on the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me see the handwriting. Yes. Mr. Zivanovic, let me be clear, if I did not see this order, and I did not since it was unavailable to me ... I'd like to see the last page to see the distribution list. I am positive that I was not on the list. Therefore it is certain that I did not change it and I did not have the right to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the last page. Let us go back -- let us go to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let's see the distribution list, please. In addition to the units mentioned, it was distributed to the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade was represented by Commander Blagojevic. It was sent to him. There was no basis for me to make any changes in the order sent to the commander by the Drina Corps command, Mr. Zivanovic. I state that firmly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go back to the front page of the document, the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that based on this order, the Bratunac Brigade issued its own order for combat activities, it is Exhibit 3085?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 3025.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I saw it together with the other documents received from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it your claim that you did not know of such an order at all and that you did not have an opportunity to see it before operation Srebrenica began and that you did not see it until you were detained in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I said in my previous testimony, the order compiled by the Bratunac Brigade commander was not forwarded to me and I did not participate in its drafting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you saw this order for the first time, as well as the previous one, here in the Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct. Could we please see the last page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be wise to see the penultimate page of the document as well.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The same as in the previous order. The original was sent to -- now the page is gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, if we could go back to the last page again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the original was to kept at the archives of the brigade. It was sent to the commands of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th Infantry Battalion and to the brigade Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now go to the penultimate page because the issue of prisoners is referred to there. You will see the third item of the order. It says the area of assembly of POWs and war booty, collection is the area of Pribicevac, et cetera, et cetera. You knew nothing of this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't know about the decision of my commander, that he had determined that Pribicevac would be the area of collection of war booty and the assembly of POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. The day before yesterday during examination-in-chief, the Prosecutor showed the document of a commission of the government of Serbia. I don't think we have the number of the -- Republika Srpska. I don't think we have the number in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Zivanovic repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you repeat the number, please, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You probably recall having contact with them. It was in the Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: With who?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: With members of the commission of the government of Republika Srpska that was investigating -- that were investigating the crimes surrounding Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: They put certain questions and answers were provided by you. Let us go to item 5, please, of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] it is page 9 in the B/C/S. And page 8 in the English version, the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You will see that, among other things, Miroslav Deronjic was under the existing document superior to Dragomir Vasic. You will see that at the beginning of the page?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If I may have a moment to read it. Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It also says that Miroslav Deronjic in the second stage of the operation was the key person who participated in the making of all decisions and was privy to all events that had to do with the civilian population and POWs who had been separated in Potocari. That's what it says?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, my impression is that you didn't mention that in the statement of facts. I even couldn't find anything like that in your previous testimonies or interviews?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I talked and testified about what I was being asked, so if you are asking me about this, I stand by it. If you need further explanation, I can do that within my best ability. Why I wrote that and why I think that answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, you don't have to give me explanations, I believe that this is what it is. I'm just interested to know, was there any reason why this was omitted from the statement of facts?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think at least five times yesterday I told you that when I had this interview with the OTP, I didn't know, nor do I know today, what was and what should have been done. I'm not a lawyer. The only thing that I can tell you is that I hold responsible my lawyers for failing to include what they should have included in it. I know no other reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to break now, Mr. Zivanovic, and you conclude soon after we start again. 25 minutes time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, are you related to -- or were you related to Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we were. He was my brother-in-law. Actually, my cousin was married to him, not my sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And I assume that you were -- that you had a good relationship?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were in the Detention Unit here approximately the same time when he was?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And as far as I could see, a very short time elapsed between your plea agreement and his plea agreement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly when he concluded his plea agreement, but you may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Within this plea agreement of Mr. Deronjic, are you aware that the OTP has decided to suspend any prosecution of him for the events in Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know any details of his agreement, and I had no opportunity to see it, therefore, I cannot give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, correct me if I'm wrong, but it seems to me that the portion of the statement that you gave to the government of Republika Srpska that we read before the break, had a significant impact on the outcome of the proceedings against Mr. Deronjic when it relates to the 1995 events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is not up to me to judge what would happen otherwise. I really cannot offer any opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is also my impression that what you wrote in this statement, you have decided to do so only after the first instance harsh sentence was pronounced against you. I think it was 27 years of imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I gave this statement when I was asked. I hadn't been asked anything about this previously, and I said that only at the moment when they asked me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at 1D1378.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a document or the note of -- Official Note compiled by the commission of the government of the Republika Srpska relating to the conversation or the interview they had with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we please move to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see this -- there was no audio recording of this conversation because the OTP opposed that move. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember what attitudes that the OTP took towards this interview. I only know that I accepted to give this interview and what the OTP said, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just want to correct a -- I'm sure my friend just misread the document, but it's quite clear in the document that it says that "the guard service of the Detention Unit did not allow me to bring in any technical equipment because we had not asked the Prosecutor's Office for permission." So -- and that is in the English at the top of page 2. I am afraid I don't have the B/C/S version in front of me. So I just want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The version is on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to make sure that this excerpt is being quoted accurately. As far as I know, OTP was never consulted in connection with this interview. So it's not the OTP making the decision, it's simply -- according to this document anyway, it's the UN Detention Unit not permitting recording equipment because the OTP had not been consulted in advance of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Thayer. Are you in agreement with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'll read the first paragraph of -- on this page. [Interpretation] "I note that Mr. Bacon and I had planned to record this conversation on the dictaphone, but the guard service of the Detention Unit did not allow us to bring in any technical equipment because we had not received permission for that from the Office of the Prosecution of The Hague Tribunal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But you've read that but you also have a statement from the OTP as to what their position was; namely, that they were never consulted. So let's proceed. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not -- [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. I mean, the Prosecution has made the position clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While you have stuck to what is contained in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 2 in my opinion is much more important. It says as follows: "As far as the interview with Momir Nikolic is concerned, due to the huge volume of the material and the facts and that the Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal had conducted an interview with the above-named that lasted seven days, we suggested to him that he himself offered new information that he hadn't conveyed to anyone before." This is where I'm going to stop because I would like to ask you, is it true that at the time you had offered to provide this commission with fresh information that you hadn't conveyed to anyone else before that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't believe so. Everything I had to say to them I told them. Everything they asked me and I knew the answers, I told them, and everything they asked me to write down, I submitted to them in writing. So that would be my answer. Whether there was something new that went beyond my interview with the OTP and they asked me about that, I really cannot tell you. It was a long time ago, and after all, you have it all in writing. And as for these qualifications, it is not up to me to decide and on what basis they made these conclusions. You have to ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here explicitly that these people from the commission had said that you volunteered to give new information that you had never conveyed to anyone else. I'm just asking you about this particular portion. Is it true that you volunteered to provide them with fresh information that you hadn't disclosed to anyone before?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I can ascertain that I didn't say anything specific to them that was not previously discussed either with my lawyers or with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Further on in this paragraph it reads as follows: "Because Mr. Bacon promised him with full responsibility that if these were crucial -- if this were crucial information, he can influence the Appeals Chamber in sense of reducing the sentence due to his cooperativeness." Did Mr. Bacon tell you anything of that nature during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't remember any promises being made concerning the reduction of my sentence or my status. What is written here, I'm almost 100 per cent sure, has nothing to do what we actually discussed, especially it's impossible that Mr. Bacon was the one who could help me reduce my sentence. I don't recall any such thing. Please believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is my impression that this was not an insignificant episode if something like that was offered to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course, I would have remembered such a thing, such a hugely significant thing that has to do with the duration of sentence and any assistance, possible assistance with it. If it had happened, I would have gladly told you about it. And let me add this, never during or after this conversation was any assistance offered or rendered to me in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say then, and correct me if I'm wrong, that neither you had volunteered to supply new information disclosed to anyone -- that you didn't disclose to anyone beforehand, nor did Mr. Bacon promise you that if you supplied fresh information, he can exert some influence and achieve the reduction of your sentence because you acted in a cooperative way?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my opinion, such discussions and such agreements never took place. This is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, it is my impression that precisely at that time one piece of new information that you disclosed that was unknown before that was exactly what I read to you about Mr. Deronjic, the answers that you gave about the role of Mr. Deronjic in the operation of the transportation of the civilians from Potocari and dealings with the prisoners who were separated there. So it is my impression that this would be one of those new pieces of information that you disclosed at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have my comment on that, and I can assure you that what relates to Mr. Deronjic, his role and his responsibility and his importance was no secret to anyone at the time, and that cannot be qualified as any new piece of information at the time when I had this discussion with the commission. Everybody knew about that. And there's an abundance of documents that testify to the fact how important Mr. Deronjic was. What I said or wrote down cannot be described as new piece of information that can either augment or diminish the importance of Mr. Deronjic. Just look at the decision on the appointment of Mr. Deronjic issued by President Karadzic, and you yourself can see what it means and you can draw your own conclusion from that document, and compare it to what I said to the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if after giving the statement of facts, did you offer to disclose any information to the OTP relating specifically to the events in Serbia and eastern Bosnia in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that, but I'm not sure. I don't know whether it took place after the interview with the commission. That's the only thing I'm not sure about. That's the timing, when was it when I discussed this issue with the OTP. But it is true that I told the OTP that I can, as far as I know and as far as my presence in Bratunac in 1992 is concerned, can provide certain information relating to the then prevailing situation, but I honestly cannot tell you whether that took place before my interview with the commission or after. Yeah, in Bratunac where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you that happened before your interview with the commission. If you wish, you can look at document 7D629, it's a letter written by the OTP in which they say that your offer would become a constituent part of the plea agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I believe what you are saying and I can confirm that I was willing and prepared to provide the information that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Nikolic, I'm going to move now to the last topic that I would like to discuss with you, and shed some light on it. At the very beginning we both noticed that you wanted to reach a plea agreement with the OTP, not immediately when you were brought here, but after certain period of time had elapsed. I have noticed that in your efforts to achieve this agreement, among other things, you even accepted responsibility for something that you hadn't done. One of those things was that you had ordered the killings in Kravica. Could you kindly please look at Exhibit 4485. That's a joint submission, and I believe actually it's annex B to the joint commission -- submission made together between you and the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it's all right. I know now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that initially you wrongly stated to the OTP that you had ordered the executions in Sandici and in the warehouse in Kravica on the 30th of July, 1995. Can you give us the explanation for the reasons behind your act?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The OTP and I had lengthy discussions about numerous topics and issues that related to the topic of our conversations. At one point towards the end of one of these conversations, a misunderstanding occurred and there was a kind of stalemate. Something happened with which quite simply, I did not agree, and I could not concede that I had any role in the events and in the crimes that were committed in Kravica. The OTP probably, this is just my opinion, was under the impression that I did take part in these events, and they insisted on it. At one point, the whole agreement came into question and we were nearing the end of our talks. Quite simply, I was very keen to reach that agreement because I had no other way out. And slightly frustrated and agitated when Mr. McCloskey asked me, did you take part in that, I just said yes, yes, I did. I ordered the killing of those people. That's what happened. Immediately thereafter, I asked the talks to be suspended. I met with my Defence lawyers, I told them what I had done, what mistake I made, that it was because of the state of mind that I was in, and I asked my lawyers to tell them that I wished to apologise to the OTP that I told them untruth, that what I said was false, and that I wanted to apologise to them. We broke for a day and then the next day we met again with the OTP. I apologized to Mr. McCloskey and his team for telling them something that was not true, and I reiterated my statement and I'm saying it again today here that I had nothing to do with that event. After that, Mr. McCloskey and his team told me that it would be necessary for the sake of truth to draft an annex to the agreement in which everything that happened would be described. I said that I was ready to sign it because I made -- had made a mistake by saying something that was not true, and then I was prepared to bear any consequences of that act. And this is how it ended. We continued our talks after that and I did my best until the very end to speak the truth and to tell them everything I knew to the best of my ability. There was another problem that had to do with a photograph. Initially, I admitted that it was me in that photograph, and I can tell you that at that time I was really convinced that I was in that photograph that was shown to me. However, my lawyers after everything took place checked this photograph on the [indiscernible], found the other person who was in the photograph, located him, took a statement from him, and this persons name was Milo Savic. I think I'm correct. He was member of a special MUP brigade in the Sandici sector. They brought me proof and his statement, and my Defence lawyers handed all of that to Mr. McCloskey and his team. This is what actually and truly happened. I would like to say once again that I'm sorry for making this mistake. I shouldn't have said that I participated in something that I didn't, and that was my mistake and I would like to apologise to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you did this because the OTP had insisted on establishing a link between you and the events in Kravica. Now, I don't understand if they insisted on that and you conceded that you had given these order, then how come that so easily they accepted your denial, subsequent denial? So in a nutshell, I find it a little bit odd, there is some discrepancy because as you said, it was them who insisted on your involvement in the crime in Kravica and then after you confessed that, the following day they decided to give up on that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You really have to ask that question of the gentleman from OTP. I don't blame the OTP for what they did. They were doing their job. I blame my Defence lawyers because they knew. I told them everything, the whole truth about what had happened and what I had been involved in, and that is contained later in my statement and in my testimony, and I don't hold the OTP responsible at all. They were merely doing their job. I made a mistake. I admitted to making a mistake, and I had serious consequences because of that. I couldn't rectify it in any other way because the mistake was there, and I was prepared to face all the consequences. I suppose that that greatly contributed to my being sentenced to the term of imprisonment that I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now you are saying that you are actually not blaming the OTP for that, but that you are blaming your lawyers. I understand that. But I also understand that you previously said that you did this because you were irritated and frustrated by such an insistence on the part of the OTP, and then only afterwards you notified your lawyers about what you did?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no. My lawyers were all the time with me while the conversation was going on. My Defence lawyers were in the same room with me and the OTP. I said after we broke the meeting, I had one day off. There was a holiday here in Holland, and I talked to my Defence lawyers in the Detention Unit on which occasion I asked them to get in touch with the OTP and convey everything that I told you awhile ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I -- can you please clarify because it's totally unclear to me that it was you who ordered the murder in Sandici?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That happened within the same statement and the same context. That was this part or area which is close by, and it has to do with the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In late 2007 you were supposed to appear as witness in this case as a Prosecution witness?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you meet with any OTP representatives in the preparation stage for that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what the status of that portion is with the Prosecution, but in any case, we had contact prior to my testimony. I did have contact with certain members of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many times you met with them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Twice in Finland.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you accept to testify in this case?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why it was that you did not testify at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was never explained to me why I was not called to testify. We talked but no one from the Prosecution ever told me what the reason was behind them withdrawing me as witness. In any case, I was notified by the Finnish authorities that I am no longer going to appear as a Prosecution witness. As for any reasons, you should ask that of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any problems in terms of your arrival here? Did you caution them as to any of your medical problems being a hindrance of any sort?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: All of us who are in prison have medical problems, standard medical problems of inmates. I have symptoms even now. In any case, in my view, medical problems are not important enough. It is true that I am of better health now than then, but even then I would have been able to testify. Maybe perhaps not in a long stretch, but I could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of those conversations, do you remember any representatives of the OTP asking you for any notes of yours?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I met with them, I think I had with me the notes I handed over here in terms of proofing -- actually, in terms of my own preparation. I then believed, as I do now, that it is a working document and that I am under no obligation to hand it over to anyone. They did not insist. I simply told them what it was about and they did not even have a look at it. I did not give them the documents and they did not insist. It was the same notes I handed over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The same notes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We were notified by the OTP about the conversation you had with them. In the course of proofing, it was on the 27th of September, 19th of October, 2007. It is 4480, that is the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, please. Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said -- it's not marked, but I will para-phrase in brief. Among other things, you said that you accepted your responsibility for the crime in Kravica because your then attorney told you that without that the OTP would not conclude a plea agreement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That took place during a break. After I had told them that I had nothing to do with that and that I didn't know what happened. My attorney, Londrovic... There is one thing, this could be my attorney's, Mr. Londrovic's, version of events, although I have my doubts as to whether that was indeed the position of the OTP, because on numerous occasions, I managed to realize that Londrovic was saying thing that was good for him and that he did not want to stand up for me in order to do his job. I cannot confirm that this is correct, that it was the OTP position. My doubts go to Londrovic rather than to the OTP, this sentence that says that the OTP put that as a precondition, otherwise there would be no plea agreement. I doubt that, given that Mr. Londrovic tricked me numerous times concerning what we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just on -- my question was different. I'm interested in whether indeed you said to the OTP during the proofing sessions that you accepted responsibility for the crimes in Kravica because your attorney had told you that without that the OTP would not conclude a plea agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You will recall that you testified in the Blagojevic case on the 19th of September, 2003. It is 7D509. Page 1595. Line 5. You mentioned the photograph, and I won't go into that anymore. I will read another portion where you say: "[In English] This statement I made that is in the statement provided, I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that it was my decision, that was an assessment that I made, and at that time I was not influenced by my lawyers or by the Prosecution. No one exercised any pressure on me at that time. No one exerted any pressure on me. Once the agreements with the Prosecution had already advanced, I came to the decision that there would be no agreement, and I really wanted to obtain an agreement. I made a mistake. I admitted something I hadn't done because I wanted to obtain such an agreement. I accepted responsibility for something that I had not done. I accepted a great degree of responsibility." [Interpretation] This testimony is quite different from what you have been telling us here. Can you explain why.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In essence, this is the same thing I said today. The only difference being that at that time I did not want to blame neither my lawyer nor anyone else for practical reasons. At the time, I had no other solution. The only thing I had were Londrovic and Kirsch, the two lawyers. I didn't want to explain in broad terms what had taken place. And in essence, that is true. I made the decision irrespective of what my lawyers said and irrespective of the OTP asking anything or not. I still stand by what I said, that it was my decision, I decided on it, I accepted that responsibility, and I bore the consequences of that decision. It is true that this is somewhat different, that I said that there was no pressure exerted at the time in the sense of anyone insisting or asking of me to do that, but simply my knowledge, my awareness that the talks were coming to an end was sufficient. Everything I knew I said. All of the documents I had were handed over to the Prosecution. I had no other way out. I had no other means of defending myself. And it is true, I did care about reaching the agreement. There was no other way out for me. That's the truth. I reiterate, I made the decision irrespective of my lawyer, irrespective of any misunderstandings with the Prosecution. It was I who made the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say in essence you don't see any difference between the Blagojevic testimony and what you are telling us here?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't see any material difference. I simply acknowledged what I had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A few months later, you were called it to testify in the Kravica case before the BiH court. On that occasion, you expressly stated that you did not wish to appear as a Prosecution witness. You did not want to specify your reasons then. Could you do that now?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I submitted the reasons to the BiH court. I explained to them in writing the reasons why I did not wish to appear as a Prosecution witness before a BiH court. Why was that? In the summons I received in the prison in Finland, it said that I was being summoned by the BiH court to appear as a witness in the proceedings. I received a similar summons while I was in the Detention Unit in Scheveningen, and I responded through the Tribunal's services, letting them know what my reasons were for not wishing to appear. The basic reason was because I believed that I was under no obligation to appear before that court. I undertook an obligation to appear as a witness of the Prosecution before the Hague Tribunal and in The Hague. Once I had concluded the agreement and took over that responsibility -- or, at that time, there was no BiH court. The other reason was this, I am no lawyer, no jurist, but I did know that in order for a BiH Prosecutor to have me appear as his witness, he would have to have my consent. Also, any circumstances of my testimony and contents of it would have to be explained to me previously and that I should have standing contact with the Prosecution, et cetera, et cetera.
