All of those things were not in place. I did not receive any request. I did not give my consent. I was merely summoned to appear as witness. Before a court in Helsinki, I said that given what I had conveyed to the BiH court, I simply did not wish to appear as a Prosecution witness, although, I wished to be helpful in the shedding of light on some things that I could testify to. Therefore, I said that I was willing to appear as a court witness in order to be cooperative so that no one could tell me, See, now he is refusing to testify. I don't know whether that could cause any problems for me, perhaps not. But I simply said If possible, I will appear as a court witness and I will respond to your questions. Even without any preparation. I had no documents, no papers based on which I could prepare myself for the testimony. That is the truth behind the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You stated the same position in the Trbic case, and you also testified before the BiH court?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is my impression that you were ready to testify to say what you knew on that occasion. Why was it so important for you not to appear as a Prosecution witness? Did you have some sort of misunderstanding with them, a problem with them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. There were no problems with the Prosecution. You have to understand that the role of a witness is an ungrateful one. No one wishes to take on obligations on top of everything they already have. I know that if I were to testify in one proceedings, it would just go on. There would be a series of that, and each new trial would have me. I'm neither of sufficient health to appear as many times, and there are some other circumstances in the gaol where I am, I'm alone there without anyone or anything. Without documents, without anything that I could count on to have quality preparation for that type of testimony. Those were my reasons. Save for the obligation I took over towards this Prosecution, I did not wish to take on any new responsibilities to testify before the BiH court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will share with you the reasons of which we were notified by the Prosecution in terms of their withdrawal of your name from the witness list. It is the 2nd November, 2007.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Zivanovic please repeat the number of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 17398, line 14. 2nd November, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: "[In English] Mr. McCloskey: We can be in open session for this. "Mr. President, as I think you are aware, about two weeks ago we a proofing session with Momir Nikolic. Julian Nicholls met with him and from that proofing session it has arisen that Momir Nikolic has become adverse to the Prosecution's case. He made statements at that proofing session that we don't believe are credible, and in reviewing his overall situation, we have decided on balance to withdraw him as a witness." My question is, do you agree with the view provided by the Prosecution? I don't know how "adverse to the Prosecution," the phrase, was interpreted to you, but I hope you understand.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: So what is your question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is, do you agree with this position of the Prosecutor concerning your attitude or position towards them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have neither the right nor do I wish to comment an OTP assessment. What they say is their position. I responsibly state here that I was never hostile to the Prosecution. I strove to be cooperative in any aspect, and there's one thing that I did not agree with in the plea agreement, and that is what I added in the supplemental statement. This only concerns those matters which I believed could or should not be ascribed to me. The way it is formulated and the words used did not reflect what I had done, and my true participation in that operation. Such formulations were, for example, organising an operation, assisting with coordination, coordination, oversight over units, control. Those were the things that I believed I did not do. They could not be ascribed to me, and it is specifically a duty of commanders. To reiterate, there was no adverse position to the Prosecution and whenever they deem necessary for me to appear as a credible witness, I will accept since I'm under that obligation. As for the things we disagreed on I tried to offer rules of service to the Prosecution which I did not have when I talked to them. Once I got by that book when I saw what the terms really mean, I realised that it was impossible. I was merely trying to avoid having to take on that type of responsibility which stems from that phraseology. Everything else I said in the statement, in my conversations with the Prosecution, and in my testimonies I am ready to repeat to the extent that I can recall. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you gave no reason to the Prosecutor to conclude that your position towards them was an adverse one or that your statements were not credible?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: To repeat, I do not wish to interpret what they thought. Had I been invited as a witness by the Prosecution, I would have behaved the same way as I did in other trials. I would try to give my maximum to explain what I believe was the truth and to explain my participation. Mr. Zivanovic, I would also strive to say, to tell the truth about the participation of others since I do not wish to bear responsibility for the things I did not have anything to do with. And to add at the end, I do not wish to minimise my role. Never did I say to the Prosecution and never did I think that I should try to represent myself as if I were someone who knew nothing and participated in nothing. I acknowledged the extent of my participation, but it should reflect my true participation, and as I've always said, I'm prepared to bear the consequences of the things I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it may be helpful to the Chamber if I could just place a couple of the events -- testimony events in chronological order for the Chamber. We've heard reference to two trials, and I think my friends will agree if I can just place the dates of those testimony in the record so the Court has an idea of when these events occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic testified via videolink in two cases, the first one was the Kravica case in the state court, that was 6th February, 2008. He then testified again via videolink in the state court in the Trbic trial, and that was on 1 September, 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay thank you. Do you agree to that Mr. Zivanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And other members of the Defence teams? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ostojic, the break will be at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is John Stojic, and I represent Mr. Ljubisa Beara along with my colleague Predrag Nikolic here. I'd like to discuss with you what I consider to be multiple, repeated, and persistent lies, half truths, and intentional omissions that you have given evidence upon in other cases as well as in this case. Sir, is it true that in fact when you look at the very exhibit that was just immediately shown to you, tab B of your statement of facts and plea agreement, you identify three particular falsehoods, as you call them, or lies. One which was the identification of yourself in a photograph that was untrue; two, your participation in executing orders relate together the Kravica massacre; and three, your participation and giving orders for the murders at Sandici. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I explained all of that to Mr. Zivanovic already. And I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to repeat it, but what I see when I look at tab B, which is P4485.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if we can have that please placed on the screen for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I see in fact that you have two other lies within that statement or declaration. Would you agree with me on that? In addition to those three, so that would make it five?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You have to tell me what it is that you disagree with, and please refrain from insulting me, if possible. If it is falsehood, then it is falsehood, I'm prepared to answer each and every question of yours but, if you insist on insulting me, I will insult you back, so I'm kindly asking you not to do that. I will answer your questions, but please refrain from insulting me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, and Mr. Nikolic, one moment, please and do heed my advice. Because everyone has got his own style and one's style sometimes is conditioned by the experience had and particular court forum. Mr. Ostojic, I suggest to you be less aggressive with the witness. No one likes being called a liar. He has given an explanation for good or for bad to Mr. Zivanovic as to why he made certain statements previously. And to you, Mr. Nikolic, I strongly advise to keep your cool. Mr. Ostojic is here carrying a responsibility that he has towards his client. He has a right to put a certain question. He has no right to insult you, but again, I mean certain terms can interpreted differently depending on the person who is hearing them. So I suggest you keep your cool, both of you, and that you, Mr. Ostojic, try to be cool as well and avoid using aggressive language.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, would you prefer - just so that I'm clear on this - that I don't use the word "lie" and instead use the word "falsehood," would that be okay? Can I use the word "falsehood" when I describe these instances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's give this --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- go straight to the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's look at Exhibit P4485 which should be on your screen. In the middle of that exhibit which you've read, and you've already testified earlier this week on Tuesday, that everything on this exhibit is true and accurate, you wrote, you state, and sign: "I voluntarily informed my lawyers and the Prosecution that I had made the false statements." Do you see that? Should be approximately eight lines from the beginning of the text?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: What we have here is a kind of clumsy wording in my language, so to speak. It says, Yes, [indiscernible] that is a Prosecutor, but there was nothing for me to inform my lawyers about this because we discussed this numerous times previously. I won't like to change anything, but I did inform my lawyers after the fact that what I had said was not true. But that was part of the package of the -- or the answers that I gave to Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I do recall --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: -- Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, thank you. I do recall some of your testimony just moments ago where you said that it was your decision, therefore, voluntarily, a day later because there was a holiday here in Holland, that you came to your lawyers and to the Prosecution and admitted this falsehood. But what I want to ask you is, do you remember in October or September of 2007 when you told the Prosecutor something entirely different, and you informed them, sir, that in fact it was the Prosecutor who came to you and said that they had a credible witness who confirms that you were not present at the Kravica warehouse massacre, and it was only at that time that you indeed then admitted the truth and said you didn't participate or give orders for that massacre? Do you remember telling the Prosecution that at all in September or October of 2007?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know the exact dates. I remember that there was discussion about this formulation as you quoted it. I don't know when and to whom I said that, but I do know and I remember a conversation with my lawyers --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me help you maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we can have P4480 on the screen for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If I may finish, please. I'd like to finish my answer. I remember my conversation with my lawyers that took place immediately after this took place, and I remember Mr. Londrovic telling me the following, Mr. Nikolic, the Prosecution has irrefutable evidence that you had not taken part in that and do not crucify yourself unnecessarily. End of quote. This is what I remember as regards this statement. As far as the confession to the Prosecution is concerned, the following day was a day off and then the day after when we met, of course before that I had met with my lawyers in the Detention Unit, I admitted to the Prosecutor -- Prosecution to what had happened and I told them the truth, that I really actually hadn't been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Slightly, with all due respect, is another version that it was your lawyers who told you that there was uncontroverted evidence that you did not participate in Kravica. But let's look at what the Prosecution said when they met with you in 2007 October.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if we could have P4480 on the screen, please. Or on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if -- because you have some trouble with dates, just if we could look at the first page and if you can see, sir, this is a supplemental information sheet generated by the Office of the Prosecution dated the 23rd of October, 2007, and in the first and second paragraph of the body of this exhibit, it has two dates identifying that the Prosecution met with you, where you're detained, on the 19th of October, 2007, as well as on the 27th of September, 2007. Do you recall them meeting with you at or about those two dates?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn to the last page of this document -- which is page -- oh, I'm sorry. The second page of the document. In English it would be the last paragraph or bullet point, and specifically the very last sentence in that bullet point. And I'll read it into the record so that you can find it, sir, so just let me know when you found it. It says -- and this is now the Prosecution, sir, identifying their conversation or relaying it with you in your -- from your prison cell. It says: "After stating that he was responsible for Kravica, the witness claims that he was told" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, make sure the witness is following in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's why I started reading it so that the witness can find the spot. It's the last bullet point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it is that important.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It would be the next page in B/C/S. And it's -- you have to scroll down just slightly, it would be that paragraph there. Where it starts with the bullet point "sredok [phoen]" and then it's the last sentence in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, let me just read it so you can follow along, but I think we have it, and I'll stop halfway so that you can just tell me if the Prosecution was accurate in what they wrote reflecting their discussion with you: "After stating that he was responsible for Kravica, the witness claims that he was told one day later that there was a reliable witness for the Prosecution who stated that Momir Nikolic was not at Kravica. The witness then admitted the truth, that he was not at Kravica during the killings." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Reconcile for me the differences in your view as to what happened when you purportedly voluntarily informed your lawyers and the Prosecution that you had made a mistake. Initially you said that it was your decision and only yours, then you told us just recently now that it was your lawyer who told that you there was an abundance, of -- I forget the word you used, of information suggesting that you were not at Kravica. Now, from this record it seems that you are informing the Prosecution that your recollection is that there was one witness that the Prosecution proffered which showed that you were not in Kravica. Which of the three might be accurate, if at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you have asked me a large number of questions at once. I don't know if your intention was to make this issue as complicated as possible. I don't want to repeat the whole story that I already told about what I told Mr. Lazarevic -- I apologise, Mr. Zivanovic. However, I'd like to confirm that in all these situations regarding all the questions, and I don't think it's anything unusual because I spoke with my lawyers on numerous occasions. I don't see anything special or anything unusual here about my conversations with my lawyers and what my lawyers conveyed to me after discussing things with the Prosecution during the breaks. Of course, I can't recall all the details. It's been a long time ago, and I cannot put all this into an ideal context. I can only tell you what really happened. Concerning this whole situation, my lawyers and I debated these issues that you mentioned. There were some misunderstandings between myself and the gentleman from the OTP about my involvement or lack thereof. I claimed then and I still claim that I did not participate, and why I made this confession, I already explained, that my lawyers were participating in that whole process is true, that we discussed all the possible scenarios, it is also true, and that is all I can tell you. Now, if you want me after all this time to remember every minute of the conversation and every word spoken between my lawyers and me, I'm not capable of doing that. If you also want me to now quote what the OTP had said and to tell you what they discussed among themselves, this is beyond me and that's my answer to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you and I wouldn't put you through a memory test. All I wanted to know really is, did you quote voluntarily -- you, Mr. Nikolic, did you voluntarily inform the Prosecutor and your lawyers that you had made these false statements? And we're talking about those three, apparently, that you've identified. Did you do it voluntarily or did the Prosecution convince you that you were not being fully truthful, or did your lawyer tell you that there was an abundance of evidence showing that you weren't at Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I categorically state here that I told my lawyers. After all this ended, they immediately came to visit me in the Detention Unit, and I told them that what I had said before was not true. There was no need for me to inform my lawyers. I'm telling you again, we talked about this on numerous occasions, and they knew very well that I was not involved in that. My lawyers and I at the next meeting informed Mr. McCloskey that that was not true. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Before the break, if I could just ask this question, maybe you could ponder it if it's going to be a long answer. If we look at 4485, what I consider to be the fifth falsehood or untruth, even though you signed it, is towards the bottom of that 4485, it says "neither my counsel nor the Prosecution ever suggested" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, let him follow the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You see that, sir. It's four lines from the bottom, it should be. And let me again begin, and I'll stop halfway so that you could find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: "Neither my counsel nor the Prosecution ever suggested..." Do you see that sentence or that portion of that sentence, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then I'll read it into the record so we have it: "Neither my counsel nor the Prosecution ever suggested in any way that I'd be untruthful." Reconcile for me, if you will, sir, your comments and your testimony about Mr. Londrovic, wherein he apparently told you, at least according to the Prosecution and what you said, that you have to accept responsibility for the Kravica warehouse and that unless you do so, there will be no plea agreement. If it's true what you signed here that no one exerted or suggested to you to be untruthful, how would you identify what you claim Mr. Londrovic told you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can put it quite simply like this, Mr. Londrovic is my lawyer. I don't know -- it's written here that there was no pressure exerted. Of course there was no pressure exerted because our people have a saying that for an intelligent person, even mosquitos buzzing is music. So if something was suggested to me, then it was an indication and a warning to me that something was going on, and that there was a certain stalemate. Therefore, I don't believe that my lawyer did his job properly. Let me tell you one more thing. As for the wording and the drafting of this statement, I had no part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just one -- if I can just have this question we can wrap this section up. So is it true or false this statement that I read from Exhibit P4485, did your counsel suggest in any way that you be untruthful?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. He didn't suggest to me to tell a falsehood. He simply told me that there was a problem, whether I was involved in the events in Kravica or whether I wasn't, and that that posed a problem. And that is the only way I can construe this. What is more important to me in all of this is that the drafting of this statement and the analysis of it is something that I simply didn't have time to do because it was written and I signed it on the day when I was expected to make my plea. That was a crucial moment for me. It was up to my lawyers to take care about the language and the wording because I am not an expert, and I admit I am not an expert in legal matters, and I don't understand them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that during the entire process of your plea negotiation you were under and felt immense pressure?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, every negotiation carries difficulties with it. Throughout the whole process, I felt that it was difficult, but I didn't feel under pressure, you cannot say that. There were problems, sometimes major problem, sometimes minor problems, some disagreements, but one cannot say what you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you wouldn't categorised it as "immense pressure"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was quite clear. It was difficult for me during these negotiations, but I wouldn't qualify them as pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me show you again this exhibit that we left off on before the break, P4480. And it's actually that same paragraph that we were looking at which is page 2, the last bullet point in the English version and the third page in the B/C/S that I believe we've been look at which starts with "the witness" or "sredok." Now, this again, sir, to refresh your recollection because we did a break, is the OTP supplemental information sheet generated after their two meetings with you in their place of detention, and that first sentence in that bullet point it says -- did you find the bullet point, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: "The witness stated that he felt immense pressure during the entire process of his plea negotiations..." and then it goes on. But I want to focus on this first part of the statement there. Did you or did you not tell the Office of the Prosecutor that which they recorded in this supplemental information sheet, or were they wrong, mistaken, or simply made this up? You told that you were under "immense pressure" during the entire process of the plea negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really don't know. I will pose a counter question to you. How would you feel? Would you feel it as pressure. Would you see that as a problem. If you had to discuss such horrendous things and make a confession to committing something that was so horrible, to me that was a pressure and a burden throughout the whole period. That is why I said that I felt terrible pressure throughout these negotiations. And I also want to tell you and ask you to try and understand this. Even now while you and I are talking, I would really like to forget all of this and put all this behind. I simply don't want this to be part of my everyday life. I'm trying to forget this and this is my final answer. I have no other explanation. The negotiations themselves were a terrible pressure and a terrible burden that I experienced in the way that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: And you can interpret that anyway you like. And I have no other comment on this. Throughout the whole negotiation and the confession and the admitting to such terrible things was and constituted enormous pressure and burden, and it's up to you to construe that in the way you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This terrible pressure and enormous pressure and burden that you were under, from whom were you receiving this from?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you know what, I wasn't talking about this kind of specific pressure. The very fact and the very course that these -- on these negotiations and the confession, the fact that one had to face something that was very ugly was pressure in itself. However, the Prosecution wanted to formulate this. Even my conversations with my lawyers were problematic and constituted pressure and burden because at that time I had to face up to all those terrible things that had happened, and you know perfectly well that in a way you yourself contributed to these events, I am talking about this kind of pressure. And even after the sentencing and after going into the Detention Unit even now, I'm still feeling enormous pressure and I'm feeling terrible. Whether you can understand this or not, I really don't know, but this is what I can tell you in all honesty.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it as a result of this terrible pressure from whomever, as you identified, that that is what led you to basically accept responsibility for anything and everything including the Kravica warehouse massacre. Would that be accurate? And if you'd like, you may answer it yes or no, and then we could proceed to another line.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. That wasn't a decisive factor for me to make such a decision. The decisive factor was --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't mean to cut you off. If you want to repeat it, I think you're entitled to do that, but I don't think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said what I wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we continue to looking at that same exhibit that's on the screen, and I only read the first part of that sentence and if we just continue to read where we were reading: "The witness stated that he felt immense pressure during the entire process of his plea negotiations and that this had led him to take responsibility for the Kravica killings during his plea negotiations." Did you find that and do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All I want to know from you, sir, the Prosecution said in this supplemental information report, 23rd of October, 2007, when they met with you, that you told them this? Is it true that you told them this? Did they accurately state what you told them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have given a full and precise explanation of everything that has to do with Kravica and I have nothing further to add to that. I told you everything. How it all happened, how the negotiations went, and I really have nothing to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then let's switch to a different topic, although somewhat related involving this exhibit and others. I want to talk about what I've coined the self-professed mental illness that you might be experiencing. And you touched a little bit about it in your previous answers. Sir, is it correct that on the 27th of September and the 19th of October, 2007, you informed the Prosecution that "you strenuously complained that you were mentally unfit to testify in the instant case," that is the case OTP versus Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my conversations with the OTP, I indeed say said that I was ill, and I was ill. There were a lot of problems in the prison where I'm serving my sentence, and I told them then that I was really not prepared to take to the stand or to give any kind of statements or testimonies, and specifically I wasn't able to endure any lengthy preparations. I told them I was sick, and I was sick, so if the OTP have recorded that, then it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about did you ever tell them that you were traumatised by listening to your own audio of your testimony from the Blagojevic case? You remember telling them that you were not only mentally unfit to testify but that you were also traumatised?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I told the gentleman who came to visit me then that I simply felt very bad. I did try to listen to the recorded testimonies, but I told them that I felt very bad and that I wouldn't be able to continue listening to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you also inform the Office of the Prosecution during those two meetings that you felt or feared that you would have a breakdown on the stand if you were to come and testify?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I said so. Sorry, it was my assessment that that might happen. I was extremely exhausted. I was on the edge because of the circumstances in the detention. I wouldn't like to discuss this at this point, but in any case, I was in poor shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, sir, would you agree with the Prosecution if I told you that when they described you after those two meetings, that you were "extremely distraught"? Would you agree with that conclusion that they made?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Forgive me for asking, sir, are you willing and able to proceed here today?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I'm ready today. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you tell the OTP during your two meetings with them in September and October of 2007 that you felt under attack and that you had been undermined and betrayed by everyone?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not understand, please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During your meetings with the OTP on the 27th of September, 2007, and the 19th of October, 2007, did you inform the Office of the Prosecution and the people that were at your detention centre, or at your gaol, that you had been undermined and betrayed by everyone and that you were under attack, or you felt under attack, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember my exact words.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's look at that same Exhibit, 4480. P4480. And I think it's actually the very last paragraph on both documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So in English it's page 3, and then in the B/C/S I would ask the assistance of the Court to just show us where in e-court that last paragraph is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, it's the third sentence or so from the bottom, and I'll quote -- just quote it halfway and then when you find it you tell me and then we can proceed: "The witness explained that he felt under attack, that he had been undermined and betrayed by everyone." Just take your time and find it, and if you need I'll read it again.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I understand the gist of what you are talking about. I spoke with the gentleman of the Prosecution about feeling cheated, and primarily I had in mind the behaviour of my lawyers in the course of the negotiations, drafting of documents, et cetera. That was what I wanted to convey. I don't know if that was necessarily the way they understood, but more or less that is what I told them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, who else, other than your lawyers who you are blaming from time to time, did you feel under attack, undermined, or betrayed you, because in the report it say that you felt everyone undermined and betrayed you? Who else, if you can tell us, undermined and betrayed you, according to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Don't ask me to speculate. I know the things that took place and the way they were taking shape. I was discussing my lawyers, I felt cheated by them, and I believe that as jurists they did not stand for my interests to the extent in my view they should have and it would have been necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Anyone else other than your lawyers is really what I'm asking you, sir, thank you. And I apologise for interrupting you, but I did get that part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I really can't recall any details of the conversation, but in principle that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about the Prosecution, did you feel that they betrayed you or undermined you, and in fact made you into a Mladic? Did you ever tell that to them? And if you want you can just look at the very next sentence in that very exhibit that we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. We talked about certain words and formulations in the statement. It is true that I said this. If everything was the way it was written, that would mean I would be General Mladic. If you go chronologically, and I thought then as I do now, that we should focus on certain parts of the statement, parts of which I did not understand at the time we were concluding the plea agreement. It has to do with the words used in my statement. The words such as coordination, control, oversight, management, and command. Those are the elements. I wasn't paying attention to it during the negotiations, and I thought it was the job of my lawyers. Later on when I studied that I expressed my dissatisfaction with those words being put in that document, and I was convinced that such things should not be ascribed to me. It was in that context that I said that if all this were true, I would be at the rank of General Mladic. I was no senior officer, I was a reserve captain. That was the essence of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You don't have to keep repeating, and I think we've heard it over the last few days, that very fact that you are denying now that you were coordinating or in control or command and we got that from your supplemental sheet so there's no need for that. But wouldn't you agree with me that in your other testimonies, in Blagojevic and others, and if you'd like I can give you a cite to it probably tomorrow morning, you're the one who used the words in describing your duties and responsibilities of coordinator? Do you remember that at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is true. I used that during testimony, but I owe you an explanation as to why. Not fully understanding the word "coordination," I was simply trying to repeat what I had signed, including the formulations that were included in the statement. That was the reason why I used those terms, and it is true that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and we are going to try to stick with this document for today, so I'd like to turn to another topic within this document. Do you remember if at any time either in September or October 2007 the Office of the Prosecutor had prepared a written statement or draft of a statement that they wanted you to sign while they visited you in your prison cell?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall any such thing. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, just to finish up on the self-professed mental illness that we touched upon and then we'll go to another topic. Sir, were you ever under the care of a doctor or psychiatrist or health care professional who diagnosed you with any mental illness or illnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Nikolic, if you prefer to have any of these issues relating to your health discussed in private session or closed session, please let us know. And at the same time, may I ask what is the relevance of this question, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think that it may go to the credibility of the witness's recollection and ultimately his testimony here. If the Court -- just so the Court knows, he has testified to this very issue before and it was in open session, but I can move on if the Court wishes me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, do you wish to answer this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, there is no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Had you ever been diagnosed with a mental illness of any kind or a nervous breakdown?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I'm not a mental patient, let me make that clear. In 1992 there were certain events. I can explain if you want me to, but in any case, I was attacked by a group of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We can get to the facts of that. All I want to know, sir, is were you hospitalised as a result of that in a neuropsychiatric hospital both in Bosnia as well as for five to six months in Belgrade? We don't need, I don't think, but if you wish, go ahead, you can explain the whole story.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course I will. After that, pursuant to the recommendations of the head of the medical service, Mr. Maticic, I was sent out of Bratunac since I was physically attacked. I went to Serbia. I spent two days in a hospital in Sabac. If you need documents, I can show it to you. I was there for two days. After that, my family came and I went to Belgrade. I was taking medication in Belgrade, underwent a treatment, and then returned. To make it absolutely clear, I was on the verge of a nervous breakdown because of everything that was taking place in Bratunac. But I also wish to say that I'm not ashamed of it. It is only human to fall ill because of all the things that were happening there. I couldn't stand them, couldn't stand what was going on. After which, thank God, I recovered and returned to the Bratunac Brigade. If you want me, I can say all about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And upon your return back to Bratunac after that five to six months or so of convalescing in Belgrade, what position did attain either in the Territorial Defence or in the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I returned, perhaps I may go wrong on the date, but I'll try to be precise, I think I returned to Belgrade on the 19th of November. I think, although I'm not certain. By that time in Bratunac, the brigade had been formed. There was no longer any Territorial Defence, it was the brigade that was in place. After awhile, say a week or a fortnight later, I was assigned to the duty which I occupied until the end of the war; that is to say, head of the security intelligence organ in the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And prior to that what was your position, sir, when you were with the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was acting as the head of the territorial municipal staff. Territorial Defence municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And at that time when you were the head of the territorial municipal staff, Miroslav Deronjic was also in Bratunac; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just for my historical perspective, I think he was president of the Crisis Staff from April 1992 up to a certain point, would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There are documents you can look at. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When did, to the best of your recollection, the Crisis Staff transform into being called the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who else were members of this Crisis Staff or War Presidency after April of 1992 when it was initially instituted?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You know what, I can tell you what the functions of particular members were, but I don't remember their names any longer. I could use a document to jog my memory, but in terms of functions, there was the president of the SDS, the president of the Executive Board, the president of the assembly, or the speaker of the assembly, a head of the Secretariat of territorial -- of national defence, the commander of the staff, and I believe the head of MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that document. Let's talk about another -- and sticking with Kravica, I want to talk about a person whose name I cannot reveal to you in open session, so we'll call him PW-161.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So if I can, with the Court's permission, go into private session, and with the Court's permission if I can identify the witness to him, then I'll do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Kwon is right, we need to redact your question, and our suggestion is that we go back to private session and continue until you finish this matter in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can just have a clarification so that I don't make the same mistake again, why is it being redacted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you are safe to ask that question with his name actually in open session, but you indicated in open session that gentleman is PW-161.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the abundance of caution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This document is public document, and you identified his pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to private session

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, on another topic if you will, for our purposes here, back in 1995, could you please describe the relationship, if any, between Dragan Mrkovic and Dragomir Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. Dragomir Vasic and Mrkovic, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday, I asked the court that I would need your notes so that you can have them in front of you, the original. I would like to go over some of those notes tomorrow given that we are at the close of today's session, and particularly if you could look at your notes relating to a person by the name of Dragan Mrkovic, and I'm going to highlight for you, it's on page 3, I think, of that six-page handwritten description that you give of his testimony. So would you be kind enough to do that for me or at least bring the notes tomorrow so that we could go over that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have it here. We can deal with it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I didn't know, I didn't see it on you. Thank you. Now, from what I -- in a brief cursory review of your notes that I kind of had a chance to glance at, you kind of break it down into three sections. One section is testimony that comes from the DutchBat or the UN personnel, a second section deals with the testimony from various Bosnian Muslims, in essence, and the third group of documents which you provide a table of contents for is testimony or statements that you've reviewed from Bosnian Serbs. Would that be generally accurate? And I know there might be some exceptions to that. Is that the way you kind of broke it down?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. In the first part there is a number of orders, yes, more or less that's it. You want to discuss this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your notes and your comments regarding Dragan Mrkovic, and you'll find that in your summary of his. It's in the middle portion, if I recall, of your original binder. It looks like we are out of time, but I could still help through the usher to help you find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will adjourn until tomorrow, 9.00. Thank you.
